summary: Serving up to ~5000 rarely-invoked, latency-tolerant LLM "thoughts" from a single machine that also runs a Java game server is FEASIBLE, but only with the right architecture: a small quantized instruct model (1.5B-8B), an inference server with continuous batching + automatic shared-prefix (KV) caching, constrained JSON decoding for short outputs, and a coalescing request queue. The controlling numbers are modest: at a 60s per-agent cadence, 5000 agents produce only ~83 requests/sec and, with ~80-token JSON outputs, roughly 5k-10k decode tokens/sec aggregate â€” well within reach of a single 24GB consumer GPU running vLLM/SGLang with a 3B-8B AWQ/GPTQ model, or llama.cpp/llama-server with a Q4/Q5 GGUF. The hard constraint is co-locating this with the Java server on ONE box: the LLM wants the GPU (and several GB of RAM/VRAM), the JVM wants CPU cores and heap, so you must budget resources and, critically, design the agent layer so the LLM is invoked rarely (rules/behavior-trees decide >95% of actions) and degrades gracefully. 5000 is realistic as a POPULATION size, not as 5000 simultaneous in-flight LLM calls; the design must cap concurrent LLM-active agents via liveliness tiers.
key_facts: REQUEST-RATE MATH: 5000 agents / cadence = request rate. Every 30s -> ~167 req/s. Every 60s -> ~83 req/s. Every 120s -> ~42 req/s. These are AVERAGE rates; without smoothing they arrive bursty, which is exactly what a coalescing queue + continuous batching absorbs.

TOKEN-RATE MATH (decode-dominated): aggregate output tokens/sec = req/s x output_tokens. With short JSON outputs of ~60-100 tokens: 83 req/s x 80 = ~6,600 tok/s decode; 167 req/s x 100 = ~16,700 tok/s. Prefill is largely eliminated by shared-prefix caching (the common system prompt is computed once and reused), so the variable prefill is only the per-agent context (~150-400 tokens): 83 req/s x ~250 = ~20k prefill tok/s, but this is cheap batched-matmul work, not the bottleneck.

GPU CAPACITY (single 24GB card, e.g. RTX 4090/3090): a 3B-7B model under vLLM/SGLang with continuous batching sustains roughly 2,000-8,000+ generated tokens/sec aggregate depending on model size, quant, and batch size (7B AWQ int4 on a 4090 commonly does multiple thousand tok/s aggregate at high concurrency; 1.5B-3B models several times that). This comfortably covers the ~5k-17k tok/s targets above for models up to ~7-8B at Q4/int4, especially at the 60-120s cadences. The 30s cadence with a 7-8B model is the tight end and may need a smaller model or batching-latency tradeoffs.

MODEL FOOTPRINT on 24GB: a 7-8B model at 4-bit (~4-5GB weights) leaves ~15GB+ for KV cache. Per-agent KV cache is the real scaling limit for CONCURRENT in-flight requests, not the agent population. Short prompts + short outputs + prefix-cache sharing of the system prompt keep per-request KV small, so a 24GB card can hold hundreds of concurrent sequences. You do NOT need KV cache for 5000 agents simultaneously â€” only for the batch actually in flight (tens to low hundreds).

CPU-ONLY FALLBACK is much weaker: llama.cpp on a modern many-core CPU serves a 1.5B-3B Q4 GGUF at only ~single-digits to low-tens of tokens/sec aggregate with small batches; realistically a few requests/sec of short generations. Viable only for a few hundred low-liveliness agents or as a degraded mode, not 5000 at speed. Co-locating heavy CPU inference with the JVM also directly contends for the same cores.

STACK FIT â€” vLLM: PagedAttention + continuous batching + automatic prefix caching (enable_prefix_caching=True) + structured outputs via xgrammar/guidance (JSON schema, regex, EBNF grammar, choice). Best-in-class throughput for many concurrent requests; OpenAI-compatible server. Strong default choice on NVIDIA for this workload.

STACK FIT â€” SGLang: RadixAttention gives automatic, tree-structured prefix caching across requests (ideal when thousands of agents share one system prompt and branch), continuous batching, and structured/constrained generation; throughput competitive with or exceeding vLLM on prefix-heavy workloads. Excellent fit for the shared-system-prompt pattern.

STACK FIT â€” llama.cpp / llama-server: supports continuous/dynamic batching (-cb / --cont-batching, on by default), parallel slots (-np/--parallel N), prompt caching with KV-shift reuse (--cache-prompt, --cache-reuse N, --slot-prompt-similarity), and constrained decoding via GBNF grammar (--grammar) and JSON schema (--json-schema/-j). GGUF Q4_K_M / Q5_K_M models. Best for consumer/cross-platform (incl. non-CUDA, Metal, CPU) and easiest to run beside a Java server; lower peak throughput than vLLM/SGLang at very high concurrency but perfectly adequate at 42-83 req/s with a small model.

STACK FIT â€” TGI (HuggingFace): continuous batching + prefix caching + guided/JSON output; solid production server but heavier and generally chosen for HF ecosystem/multi-GPU rather than single-box hobby/game deployments.

STACK FIT â€” Ollama: wraps llama.cpp; easy setup and now supports parallel requests (OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL) and JSON/format-constrained output, but less tunable for maximum throughput. Good for prototyping and small tiers; graduate to llama-server or vLLM for scale.

STACK FIT â€” ExLlamaV2 / TabbyAPI: very fast EXL2-quantized inference on a single consumer GPU with continuous batching; strong tokens/sec for one 24GB card, though narrower feature set and NVIDIA-only. A viable high-performance single-GPU option.

MODEL CHOICE for cheap, in-character, structured short outputs: Qwen2.5-Instruct family (0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B) is explicitly tuned for JSON/structured output and instruction following (32K context) â€” 1.5B-3B is a sweet spot for cheap NPC chat/decisions, 7B for higher quality. Also strong: Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct, Phi-3.5-mini (3.8B), Gemma-2-2B/9B-it. Use the smallest model that passes your in-character quality bar; smaller = far more agents per box.

CONSTRAINED DECODING keeps outputs short AND parseable: enforce a tight JSON schema/grammar (xgrammar/guidance in vLLM, GBNF/--json-schema in llama.cpp) so every response is valid structured data (e.g. {action, target, line} with maxLength on strings). This eliminates parse failures/retries and bounds output tokens, directly cutting decode cost â€” the dominant term in the token math.
architecture_notes: TIERED LIVELINESS is the core architecture, not an optimization. Do NOT treat 5000 as 5000 concurrent LLM calls. Define tiers by proximity/relevance to real players: e.g. HOT (near a player, cadence 15-30s, may use LLM), WARM (same region, 60-120s), COLD (offscreen, minutes or rule-only, no LLM). The LLM budget is a fixed req/s ceiling; agents earn LLM time by tier. This makes the system scale with PLAYER attention, not raw NPC count, and degrades gracefully when the queue saturates (demote agents to rule-only).

RULES-FIRST GATING: the behavior tree / rule engine handles the vast majority of ticks; the LLM is called ONLY when rules genuinely cannot decide (novel social situation, free-form chat, high-level goal re-plan). Target well under 5% of agent decisions reaching the LLM. This is what makes the request rate 42-167 req/s instead of thousands.

COALESCING QUEUE between agents and the inference server: agents push LLM 'thought requests' into a priority queue (priority = liveliness tier + player-interaction urgency). A dispatcher drains it and submits to the server, letting continuous batching form efficient batches. Because requests are latency-tolerant (seconds are fine), you can micro-batch on a short timer (e.g. 50-200ms) to raise batch sizes and throughput. The queue also provides backpressure: when depth exceeds a threshold, shed/downgrade low-priority requests instead of blowing latency.

SHARED-PREFIX (system prompt) CACHING is essential and free: put the large, identical instructions (world rules, output schema, persona template scaffold) at the FRONT of every prompt so vLLM APC / SGLang RadixAttention / llama.cpp prompt cache computes it once and reuses the KV across all agents. Keep the per-agent variable part (this NPC's memory summary, current situation) SHORT and place it after the shared prefix. This turns thousands of long prompts into thousands of short effective prefills.

AGENT MEMORY LIVES OUTSIDE THE LLM: store each NPC's state, relationships, goals, and recent-event log in the game server / a DB (or in-process structures), and inject only a compact summary (tens of tokens) into the prompt when the LLM is actually called. Never rely on long in-context history per agent â€” it explodes KV cache and prompt length. The LLM returns a decision; the game server persists the consequences.

TOKEN BUDGETS enforced per call: cap max_tokens tightly (e.g. 32-96), constrain output with JSON grammar, and template the input so variable content is bounded. Predictable small tokens/call = predictable aggregate load and stable batching.

CO-LOCATION resource plan on ONE box: reserve the GPU for the LLM; pin the JVM to a subset of CPU cores and cap its heap so it doesn't starve the inference server's host-side work (tokenization, sampling, scheduling); leave headroom RAM. On a single 24GB GPU the LLM owns the card. If the box has a second smaller GPU, consider putting a tiny model there. Expect to tune batch size to trade latency (fine here) for throughput.

GRACEFUL DEGRADATION path: (1) rule-only fallback for any agent whose LLM request is shed; (2) dynamic cadence stretching under load (push 60s toward 120s+); (3) shrink the LLM-active population (fewer HOT agents) before letting latency or the JVM suffer; (4) optional smaller 'fast' model tier for trivial decisions and a larger model only for player-facing chat.
risks: Co-location contention is the top risk: heavy CPU-side inference work (esp. llama.cpp/CPU fallback) competes directly with the JVM for cores and memory bandwidth, and GC pauses vs inference scheduling can interact badly. Must be resource-partitioned and load-tested together, not in isolation.

KV cache, not agent count, caps CONCURRENCY. If too many requests are genuinely in flight at once (e.g. an event makes thousands of agents 'think' simultaneously), you can exceed KV cache capacity and requests queue or get preempted. Bursty synchronized triggers (all NPCs react to one event) are the dangerous pattern â€” jitter/stagger cadences and rate-limit the queue.

The 30s cadence with a 7-8B model on a single 24GB card is near the capacity edge (~16k tok/s target); leaves little headroom for player-facing latency spikes. Mitigate with a smaller model, tighter output budgets, or accepting 60-120s cadence for most tiers.
Consumer GPUs have limited VRAM for both weights and KV; a larger (13B+) model plus many concurrent sequences will not fit at good speed on 24GB. Stay <=8B quantized unless you add GPUs.

Quality risk: 1.5B-3B models can produce off-character or low-quality social text. Constrained decoding fixes parseability but not persona quality â€” validate with your actual prompts; you may need 7B for player-facing chat and a smaller model only for internal decisions.

Throughput numbers vary widely with quant type, prompt/output length, batch size, and GPU; treat all tok/s figures here as ballparks to be confirmed by benchmarking your exact model + hardware + prompt shape.

Windows-specific: vLLM/SGLang are Linux-first (best via WSL2 or Linux); on native Windows, llama.cpp/llama-server, Ollama, or ExLlamaV2/TabbyAPI are the smoother paths. If the game server must run native Windows, this influences the stack choice.
recommendations: TARGET STACK (NVIDIA, throughput-first): vLLM or SGLang with a 3B-7B AWQ/GPTQ int4 instruct model, enable_prefix_caching / RadixAttention ON, continuous batching, structured outputs via xgrammar (JSON schema). SGLang if the shared-system-prompt sharing is your dominant pattern (it usually will be). Run on Linux or WSL2.

TARGET STACK (simplicity / native Windows / non-CUDA / consumer): llama.cpp llama-server with a Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M GGUF of a 3B (e.g. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) model, --cont-batching on, --parallel set to your expected concurrent-batch size, --cache-prompt + --cache-reuse for shared-prefix reuse, and --json-schema for constrained output. Easiest to run beside a JVM. Consider ExLlamaV2/TabbyAPI if you want more single-GPU speed on NVIDIA.

PICK THE MODEL BY QUALITY BAR, THEN GO AS SMALL AS POSSIBLE: start with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (explicitly good at JSON/structured output, 32K ctx). Drop to 1.5B if quality holds (huge throughput win); step up to 7B only for player-facing chat. Always constrain output to a tight JSON schema with small max_tokens.

SIZE THE SYSTEM BY req/s, NOT agent count: budget a fixed LLM req/s ceiling (start ~50-100 req/s), enforce it via the priority queue, and let liveliness tiers allocate that budget. This decouples feasibility from the 5000 number and gives a clean knob.

IMPLEMENT: (1) rules/behavior-tree first with an explicit 'needs LLM?' gate; (2) compact per-agent memory stored outside the model, summarized into short prompts; (3) shared system prompt as a stable front-prefix for cache reuse; (4) coalescing priority queue with micro-batch timer (~100ms) and backpressure/shedding; (5) constrained JSON decoding; (6) rule-only degradation for shed requests and dynamic cadence stretching under load.

BENCHMARK before committing: run your chosen model+stack on the target GPU with realistic prompts (shared prefix + short variable + JSON output) at increasing concurrency to find sustained tok/s and the concurrency knee, THEN co-locate the JVM and re-measure. Set the req/s ceiling below the measured knee.

Treat 5000 as a population with a bounded LLM-active subset. A realistic single-24GB-box design comfortably keeps a few hundred agents 'LLM-lively' at any moment (HOT+WARM) with the rest rule-driven, which is almost always indistinguishable to players since attention is local.
open_questions: What is the exact GPU / VRAM available on the single box (24GB assumed)? Is there any second GPU? This sets the model-size ceiling and concurrency.
Does the Java game server run native Windows or can inference run under WSL2/Linux? This decides vLLM/SGLang vs llama.cpp/Ollama.
What fraction of agent decisions truly require the LLM (measured, not assumed)? This is the single biggest driver of req/s and thus feasibility.
What are the real prompt shapes: size of shared system prompt, size of per-agent variable context, and target output length? Needed to firm up the token math and KV budget.
What latency is acceptable per 'thought'? Confirmed as seconds-tolerant here; if any calls are real-time player chat, those need a higher-priority lane with tighter latency.
Expected burstiness: are there world events that make many agents think at once? Determines how aggressively to stagger/jitter cadences and size the queue.
CPU core count and how many the JVM needs vs the inference host-side work â€” required to plan co-location.
